newsitem.title: ESTONIA: INTERVIEW-ESTONIA FINMIN SETS GOALS TO CONTINUE REFORMS.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-ESTONIA FINMIN SETS GOALS TO CONTINUE REFORMS.

text.p: Estonia's Finance Minister Mart Opmann said on Thursday the reform process was continuing but more work was needed to keep inflation on a downward trend, reform pension and land systems and boost exports.

"In order to guarantee economic stability we have to make decisions to keep inflation going down and carry out pension reforms and the introduction of pension funds," Opmann told Reuters in an interview.
"And we are not satified with the current situation of land reform."
Opmann said he was particularly concerned about the slow progress in land reform which is aimed at defining ownership and registering land that was nationalised in the Soviet era.
"On the one hand we can say the tempo is high but we are not satified," he said.
"The percentage of privatised land is still very small."
Opmann said he was also looking to the problems that Estonia will face in the future such as the repayments of state and local government borrowings.
While he knows that state borrowing is low, future repayments remain a concern.

"The total value of foreign loans which have have been guaranteed by the government of Estonia form 5.6 percent of the Estonia Gross Domestic Product (GDP), which is lower than required under the Maastrich Treaty," he said.

"At the same time the IMF has drawn our attention to the fact that during the coming years we will have to pay back these loans, and in the year 2000 the total amount (of repayment due) is 700 million kroons.
"This will be a burden to the state buget and may be dangerous to us."
By the year 2000 Estonia's inflation is predicted to be lower than the current 0.9 percent a month, but this will bring its own problems for Estonia's budget.
"Inflation is going down, repayments are going up and the growth rate of the state buget is decreasing," he said.
However, Opmann believes Estonia can meet its international obligations.

The minister said he was concentrating on increasing Estonia's exports whose value remains lower than import values. In 1997 the volume of exports is foreccast at 28 billion kroons while imports are seen at 38.4 billion kroons.
"Our decision to favour GDP growth requires guarantees and support for exports," he told Reuters.
"The question lies in the development of Estonia's exports. There is a view that Estonian exports should grow. Decisions have been made to establish an the Export Agency.
"In this case the best markets are in the region such as Russian and Ukraine. There is great potential for exports from Estonia to these countries."
He said Estonia had signed free trade agreements with Latvia and Lithuania and most recently Ukraine.
"We have to start to realise these free trade agreements and the government has done quite a lot for opening up these markets to Estonia," he said.
